prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first round my position on B016 is unchanged: a single-achievement prize for the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six members agree on the scientific substance: a complete arc from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36), through receptor biology and gut-pancreas-brain signalling, to agonists with randomized outcome evidence in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. There is no maturity concern and the effect is still widening. The only live question is the third seat, and I keep it on the discovery side because the Nobel criterion in this category is the discovery of a principle. The identification of the truncated amidated peptide as the active incretin is the step on which both the human physiology and the later pharmacology depend, so a citation that names it is the most traceable in the primary literature. A single part is also the right shape. Reducing Drucker or Holst, who all six of us name, to make room for CAR-T would trade the one secure core for a second part that has an unresolved credit problem (Eshhar, Rosenberg).
statement.case_against: The attribution of the third seat is the weakest point of my own configuration. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested by the Habener group, who are outside the credited list, and the supplied record does not let me resolve it. If the committee concludes that the priority dispute cannot be settled, then a citation resting on the identification of the active form is exposed, and Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation covering development into long-acting therapies is the more defensible fallback. I also accept that a basic trio omits the engineering of liraglutide and semaglutide, which is the reason the biology reached patients. That omission can be criticised as rewarding the idea and not the drug, and I do not claim that it is a clear-cut judgment.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, argues that translation completing a discovery has been honoured in this prize, and says that contested priority makes Mojsov a weaker anchor than Knudsen's documented work on acylated analogues.
responses.response: I accept your correction. I was too quick in round 1 to treat the exclusion of industrial development as a principle, and the tradition in this prize does include translational work that completes a discovery. Your point that contested priority cuts both ways is also fair. Where I still differ is on what the contest is about. The dispute concerns who was first or co-first to identify and make the active peptide, not whether the identification mattered, and a priority dispute over a necessary step does not make the step less necessary. Acylation extended the half-life of a molecule whose activity had already been established. I keep Mojsov, but I now regard your configuration as equal in defensibility, not as the weaker one, and I would move to it if the committee records that the Mojsov claim cannot be defended against Habener.

responses.point: Perlmann prefers Knudsen as the third name because the physiology is carried by Holst and Drucker and what separates GLP-1 from other hormone discoveries is that it became a drug class; he also notes that the third seat has no clean answer.
responses.response: I agree that what makes GLP-1 exceptional is the drug class, and that Holst and Drucker already carry much of the physiological insight. I do not think that settles the seat, though. The reason the drug class exists is that the active form was identified and shown to act in humans, and a prize that names Knudsen but not that step would explain the medicine without naming its origin in the biochemistry. You are right that I cannot verify the early record from the supplied text. I would ask the committee to decide this on the primary-literature record of who identified, synthesised and tested GLP-1(7-36), not on patent history, and to treat your trio as the fallback if the record does not support Mojsov. I disagree with you on this one point only, and I do not think the disagreement is large.

responses.point: The chair asks whether B016 should stand alone or be reduced to one or two names to add a second part such as B007, and whether June and Sadelain can be recognised without Rosenberg and Eshhar.
responses.response: I would keep B016 alone. Dropping any of Drucker, Holst or the third name to fit a second part weakens the one configuration all six of us support, in exchange for a second part that has a real attribution problem. Linnarsson and Perlmann both pointed out that Eshhar's concept of the chimeric receptor is missing from the credited names, and I share that concern. June and Sadelain without Eshhar would be exposed to the same criticism as any Nobel prize that left out an originator. CAR-T is the right alternative for a later year or for a second part if the committee is willing to defend the exclusion of Eshhar and Rosenberg. On your B003 comment, I agree with you that it is a runner-up of limited strength, and I am keeping it only as a lower alternative, for the reasons below.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks the committee to say why a sequencing technology should outrank mechanism-driven discoveries with direct disease relevance such as cGAS-STING, and keeps cGAS-STING as a later candidate with clinical benefit still unproven.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge, and I will not argue that sequencing outranks cGAS-STING on principle. I put B003 among my alternatives because maturity and effect on medicine are beyond doubt, not because the committee should reward tools in general. Its weaknesses are exactly the ones you and others describe: an enabling method rather than a discovery about disease, the unresolved weight of Mayer against the Cambridge group, and commercial development by many people outside the credited three. On cGAS-STING I agree with you that the Chen and Barber pairing is the cleanest, and the absence of demonstrated clinical benefit is a matter of timing, not of doubt about the mechanism. In an alternative slot I would now rank B007 ahead of B003 and have both ahead of B005 only because B005's five-name allocation is still open. If you believe B005 should displace B003 in an alternative slot I would not object strongly, since neither is part of my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record supports Mojsov's priority for identifying and synthesising active GLP-1(7-36) against the Habener group, who are outside the credited list. This is the single question that could move my third name to Knudsen.
Whether the committee wants a citation anchored on the active peptide and physiology or on development into long-acting therapies; I consider both defensible.
Whether a prize that omits Habener is fair to the discovery, given that the three-seat limit cannot be met by any set that includes both Habener and Knudsen.
Whether B007 can be defended without Eshhar, and whether Rosenberg belongs in the same citation; this limits how far I would trade B016 names for a second part.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. No shortlisted candidate is a documented collaborator, mentor or institutional colleague. My single-cell methods rely on massively parallel sequencing (B003), which I list only as a lower alternative; I have co-authored with Linnarsson and with others at Karolinska Institutet, none of whom is a credited name, and no recusal is needed for the ballots in my preferred configuration. Shared use of sequencing does not give me a personal stake in B003, but if the committee were to move it into a prize part I would flag this overlap and abstain from deciding its credited names.
